claim: Extra, later-undone rotations in Tetris are information-gathering actions: they come early (about 400-500 ms before the final orientation), and their share rises with skill (4%, 5%, 7% of episodes for the same player). Evidence is from one lab and two players; the 1994 paper was opened in the gap search (d02): it contains NO per-skill percentages, only argument, aggregate plots and a 3-player pilot. The 4/5/7% rates come only from the 1996 paper.
agent_test: Count, in agent traces, write/run/sketch steps whose output is later discarded or revised; compare rate across easy vs hard items and across base-model strength at equal tokens. Prediction: more such steps early in strong runs, not after errors.

claim: Corrected from the 1994 full text (d02): physical rotation takes as few as 100 ms; mental rotation of a 90-degree turn is ESTIMATED at 800-1200 ms from a 3-player pilot (plus 200 ms allowed for the key press); early rotation exposes the full shape 150-300 ms sooner than waiting for it to fall into view. The earlier figures 150/200/300 ms and 1000-1800 ms came from summaries and mix these separate quantities.
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM as stated. Use token cost of the external step vs the in-head step as the analogue; measure tokens-to-correct for write-it-out vs answer-direct on the same items.

claim: Experts in Tetris rely heavily on a visible look-ahead (Next Box) rather than on rotate-to-see: with the preview hidden, elite players could not score a Tetris (11 players, paired t all >4.5). This rivals the rotation account and is a one-off observational case study.
agent_test: Ablate a visible 'next steps' plan block in the agent context at equal tokens; measure accuracy on multi-step items with and without it.

claim: Observers can tell from video whether a person is shaking a box to find out something (epistemic) or just moving it: 76.2% accuracy (d=2.12) in Exp 1, 63.7% (d=0.86) with identical box contents. This is perception of epistemic action, not evidence that it helps solving. Re-opened and confirmed.
agent_test: Low priority. Could test whether an LLM judge can label agent steps as epistemic vs pragmatic with the same split; useful only for logging.

claim: Writing intermediate steps lets language models do multi-step computation they fail at in one pass. Scratchpad: polynomial evaluation 8.8% to 20.1% (few-shot) and 31.8% to 50.7% (fine-tuned); CoT on PaLM 540B GSM8K 17.9% to 56.9%. Theory agrees: without intermediate tokens only TC0 is reachable; T steps allow circuits of size T. Gain appears mainly at large scale.
agent_test: Same items, same token budget: direct answer vs typed trace of intermediate state. Report accuracy by serial depth (number of dependent steps).
audit_note: Nye, Wei and Merrill-Sabharwal checked; TC0 statement is a bound for log-precision transformers under complexity assumptions, and the circuit-size-T result (Li et al.) was not opened.

claim: Offloading exact computation to a program interpreter beats written reasoning where arithmetic or counting is the weak point. PAL (Codex, GSM8K) 72.0% vs CoT 65.6%; GSM-Hard 61.5% vs CoT 20.1%; PoT averages about 8% (math) and 15% (finance) over CoT; Plan+Tool solver beats Plan+CoT in the Sprague analysis. Boundary: the PAL ablation where the model only simulates running the code falls to 23.2%, so actual execution is the active ingredient, not the code-shaped text.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare: CoT, code written and run, code written but result predicted by the model. Expect the third to collapse. Add a value-grounding check (PoT: 47% of failures were wrong values taken from the problem).
audit_note: Minor: PAL GSM8K 72.0 vs Codex CoT 65.6 and GSM-Hard 61.5 vs 20.1 are as stated in text (table shows 61.2); PoT 8%/15% are few-shot averages; 'simulate running the code' ablation 23.2 verified.

claim: Written reasoning helps mostly on math, symbolic and logic tasks and gives little or negative return on commonsense, perceptual or implicit-statistical tasks. Sprague: mean CoT gain symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logic +6.9, other categories +0.7; Mind your step: up to 36.3 points lost on implicit learning; Lanham: HellaSwag accuracy -4.69 with CoT. New: implicit statistical learning GPT-4o 87.5% direct vs 64.4% CoT (d08); on a current hybrid model, always-think lowers HumanEval for three Qwen3 sizes (60.4 to 59.1, 71.3 to 66.5, 79.9 to 72.6) while it raises Olympiad math 49.8 to 71.5 (d20).
agent_test: Route by task type: run a held-out set of soft/commonsense items with and without a forced write-out step; expect no gain and a token cost.
audit_note: Minor: the 36.3-point loss is o1-preview vs GPT-4o on a subset (reasoning-trained model vs direct), not CoT on the same model; 'other categories +0.7' is derived from 56.8 vs 56.1.

claim: Meaningless extra tokens do not help off-the-shelf models: filler dots gave no accuracy gain on any task in Lanham (some drops), and commercial models showed no filler benefit in Pfau. Boundary: small transformers trained from scratch with dense supervision did use filler on parallel tasks (3SUM 100%, 2SUM-Transform 94%) but not on natural tasks. So content of the written step is what carries value for current models.
agent_test: Control arm: replace the written trace with same-length neutral filler; confirm zero gain at equal tokens before crediting content.
audit_note: Pfau et al. state the commercial-model finding as citing earlier work (Sachan), not as their own test; the 'content carries the value' conclusion is an inference.

claim: The written chain is often not what drives the answer, and the dependence is task-specific. Lanham: truncating the chain leaves the answer unchanged on some tasks (answer changed under 10% of the time on ARC and OpenBookQA; over 60% on AQuA), larger models rely on it less. Science-agent runs ignore returned evidence in 68% of traces and never update beliefs in 71% (25,000+ runs, preprint, not re-opened here). Gap-search addition: Anthropic hint tests find chains admit the hint 25% (Claude 3.7) and 39% (R1) of the time (d07); sentence resampling finds planning and uncertainty sentences carry the answer, not computation sentences (d06).
agent_test: Trace ablation test: delete or corrupt step k and measure whether later steps and the answer change. Count a step as epistemic only if it does.
audit_note: Minor: Lanham's 'under 10%' / 'over 60%' are the share of times the chain changes the final answer (ARC, OpenBookQA vs AQuA); Rios-Garcia 68%/71% verified in the preprint; the truncation wording in the claim is compressed but correct.

claim: Self-review with no outside information does not help and often hurts; the same reflect-and-retry loop gains when real external feedback exists. Huang (re-opened): GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0, GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; Reflexion with unit tests or environment signal +11% HumanEval, +22% ALFWorld.
agent_test: Revision arms at equal tokens: (a) re-read own text, (b) revise after tool or test output. Prediction: (a) flat or negative, (b) positive.
audit_note: Minor: Reflexion HumanEval uses self-generated unit tests as the feedback signal; the +22/+11 are the paper's own headline gains.

claim: Interleaving actions with a written reading of the result helps in interactive tasks but not uniformly. ReAct: ALFWorld 71% best vs Act 45%, hallucination 56% of CoT failures vs 0%; but on HotpotQA ReAct 27.4 is below CoT 29.4 and below CoT-SC 33.4; empty search results cause 23% of ReAct failures. Best results came from combining ReAct with CoT-SC.
agent_test: Per-action 'what did this return, what does it change' line; compare with and without it on tasks where lookups can return nothing, and add a fallback to internal reasoning.

claim: Calling tools that are not needed costs accuracy: 0.93 unnecessary calls per query on average, accuracy down 3.29 to 14.48% on questions answerable from knowledge (re-opened and confirmed). Training fixes cut overuse (82.8% at 32B). Prompt-only fixes untested. A position paper argues for 'epistemic necessity' gating but reports no measurements. Gap-search addition: a prompt-only verbal gate carries some signal (Llama-3-8B decision accuracy 61.9% vs 50% for always-calling, d10) and a prompt-only ask-vs-act decomposition raised clarification F1 by about 0.28 but cut average task success from 28.6% to 27.0%, with REAL 32.1% to 19.2% (d11). Knowing which unknown to ask about is weak on logic and planning (40-50%, d19). Net: prompt-only gating is tested only in clarification, with a measured accuracy cost.
agent_test: Gate arm: before each external action the agent writes what unknown it would resolve and why that cannot be resolved in context. Compare calls, accuracy and tokens vs no gate.

claim: Delegating to a simulator or physics engine and feeding the result back raises reasoning on the simulated domain: Mind's Eye UTOPIA GPT-3 175B 24% zero-shot vs 38.2% few-shot vanilla; gains +18.4% / +34.2% averaged over LM sizes (abstract headline 27.9 / 46.0 is a different average, both in the paper); 1.3B with simulation 29.8% matches vanilla 175B 29%.
agent_test: Where a cheap exact simulator exists for the domain, test small-model-plus-simulator vs larger model alone at equal cost.

claim: Drawing external visual state raises accuracy on geometry, graph and spatial tasks in strong models but only when the drawing is right. Sketchpad: +12.7% math, +8.6% vision (abstract), max flow +41.3; Visualization-of-Thought: GPT-4 navigation 59.0 vs CoT 54.0 vs no-viz 35.5 but drawn state accurate only 24-26% of the time and CoT 52.5 beat VoT 49.5 on ring navigation. Weaker models gain less.
agent_test: Keep a code-side ground-truth grid; compare model-drawn sketch vs code-rendered state vs none, and score drawing accuracy separately.
audit_note: Sketchpad 12.7%/8.6% and +41.3 max flow, VoT 59.0/54.0/35.5, 24-26% state accuracy, ring CoT 52.5 vs VoT 49.5 verified; 'only when the drawing is right' is an interpretation of VoT's 65-77% correct moves given accurate states.

claim: When code cannot run a step, having the model simulate executing written code or pseudocode still beats plain CoT: Chain of Code BBH 84 vs CoT 72 vs direct 55 (text-davinci-003); Think-and-Execute beats zero-shot CoT on seven algorithmic tasks. Both are author-run reruns of the competing baseline.
agent_test: Fallback ladder: run exact code; if not runnable, write pseudocode and trace it line by line; compare to unaided CoT at equal tokens.
audit_note: BBH 84/72/55 verified in Chain of Code; Think-and-Execute beating zero-shot CoT on seven tasks verified; author-run-baseline caveat is the claim's own.

claim: A typed external memory (confirmed facts, ranked hypotheses, open questions) beats unstructured notes: SLEUTH 4-hop MuSiQue 53.1 vs ReAct 42.0 and Notes 41.7; Facts-only alone 49.9; Iris removal of information management cost 13.4 points any-medal on 15 tasks, one run each. Single-author or small-N preprints. Searched again 2026-10: no independent replication found (d22).
agent_test: State-format arm: typed blocks vs free diary at equal tokens on multi-hop items; verify format adherence by code.

claim: Structure only helps if the harness enforces it, and a late commit trigger helps only when structured state exists. GLM-5 followed the protocol on 15% of turns with a generic prompt and 99% with an adapted prompt plus runtime check (4-hop 29.9 to 48.9); a nudge at 70% of budget lifted SLEUTH 49.1 to 53.1 but left ReAct at 42.2.
agent_test: Code validates the state block every turn and forces commit at a counted budget fraction; compare against prompt-only.

claim: Short symbolic 'sketch' notes can match long prose: Sketch-of-Thought reports up to 84% fewer output tokens with similar accuracy (Qwen-2.5-32B 82.30 vs CoT 82.24 at 74.36% fewer tokens). Router-chosen paradigms; read at abstract/partial level only.
agent_test: Terse typed notes vs prose at matched accuracy; report tokens saved and spend them on a second sample.

claim: Moving the hands in a way tied to the task content lightens working memory, meaningless movement does not (Cook: N=115, beta=-.17 and -.13, p<.01; first-condition-only checks weaker, p=.057 and .02). Meta-analysis: gesture helps comprehension d=.61, production d=.91 vs observation d=.54. But with verbal analogies people recalled more when not gesturing (d=.34, N=40). So the benefit depends on task type and is not free.
agent_test: Do not force an external write-out on every task; compare content-bearing notes, filler notes and no notes on both symbolic and verbal items.

claim: The size of the benefit from external aids grows as inner capacity falls: lower working memory or spatial ability predicts more gesture and more harm when it is blocked; an external grid helps more on 4x4 than 3x3 tic-tac-toe. All of this is second-hand through Pouw et al. (2014); originals not opened.
agent_test: Scale externalisation with problem size and base-model strength; test a weaker model with and without the scaffold to see if the gap is larger.

claim: Letting people physically manipulate a problem does not reliably raise solution rates in lab tasks. Ross and Vallee-Tourangeau: word fluency high-interactivity 18.35 vs 17.02 (F(2,78)=1.94, p=.146); Spiridonov et al.: matchstick Exp 1 interactive vs static accuracy about equal (.91 vs .94 on problem A), only VR interactive sticks +0.67 log-odds (CI .22 to 1.15), other CIs include zero.
agent_test: Warns against overselling: test each external action alone for incremental gain at equal tokens before including it in the schema.
audit_note: Numbers verified; minor: Ross and Vallee-Tourangeau found time spent moving tiles did predict words, and Spiridonov per-problem models show positive effects on problem D in Exp 2 and 3, so 'not reliably' is right but not 'no effect'.

claim: Searching alternatives outside the head with evaluation and pruning gives large gains on a search task with a foothold, at many times the calls: Game of 24 GPT-4 IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, ToT b=1 45%, b=5 74% (re-opened and confirmed).
agent_test: Compare one-pass, best-of-N and pruned tree at equal total tokens, not equal calls.

claim: Partial update. A position paper (d12, Oct 2026) maps epistemic action onto LLM agents as acquire / transform / probe, but reports no measurements. Measured near-misses: in-context bandit exploration needed a code-built summary, only 1 of 48 or 72 GPT-3.5/GPT-4/Llama 2 configurations explored well (d15); in a 20-questions game thinking models gather more information per question, especially early (IG/turn 0.42 vs 0.14, win rate 0.93 vs 0.10 in the partially observable setting, d16). No study of early, reversible, undoable probes that rise with model skill was found.
agent_test: Build the trace log first (K01 test), then check whether stronger models probe earlier and more often.

claim: On a reasoning-trained model, adding a prompt that asks for more written steps gives little: GPQA Diamond o3-mini +2.9, o4-mini +3.1, Gemini Flash 2.5 -3.3 points, at +20-80% time (198 questions x 25 trials). For non-reasoning models the same prompt adds +4 to +13 points over a forced-direct answer but little (-1.9 to +6.9) over the model's default behaviour.
agent_test: Equal-token arm on the current base model: S2 notes on vs off, scored on held-out items; expect 0-3 points for reasoning-trained bases.

claim: Native thinking still matters a lot on hard math for current open models: Qwen3-235B-A22B AIME'24 85.7 thinking vs 40.1 non-thinking; Qwen3-8B Olympiad 71.5 vs 49.8. On code, always-think was lower than no-think for three Qwen3 sizes on HumanEval. So the question left open by gap 1 is not whether thinking helps but whether a second visible scratchpad adds anything on top.
agent_test: Run base-thinking vs base-thinking + explicit S2 notes on math and on code; report accuracy at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the thinking vs non-thinking Qwen3-235B numbers are AIME'24 85.7 vs 40.1 in the report's tables; the last sentence is interpretation.

claim: Executed code adds solved problems beyond text-only reasoning even in the trained regime: Qwen2.5-32B AIME 2024 67.0% (tool RL, 400 steps) vs 40.0% (text RL, 1,080 steps), response length down about 40% (ReTool); Qwen3-8B Omni-MATH-512 pass@256 82.0% vs 68.4%, 15.4% of problems newly solved vs 1.8% lost, about +9 points on non-algorithmic problems. Evidence is for trained models; prompt-only transfer untested.
agent_test: S4 arm: base model with a code run on computable sub-steps vs same model text-only at equal tokens; count problems solved only by the code arm.
audit_note: ReTool numbers verified (67.0 at 400 steps vs 40.0 at 1080; length down ~40%); Lin and Xu 82.0 vs 68.4, 15.4% vs 1.8% verified; the about +9 points on non-algorithmic problems is figure-only and was not confirmed in text.

claim: Forcing text-only step-by-step can lower a reasoning-trained model's score: o1-preview 88.2 question-only vs 81.9 all-text vs 93.3 all-code (d05); Flash 2.5 -3.3 points with CoT prompt (d01); o1-preview vs GPT-4o on implicit learning 57.7 vs 94.0 (d08, mixes model and mode). A hybrid of code and text plus a summary gave the best six-model mean (79.5 vs 72.8 question-only).
agent_test: Never make S2 notes mandatory on every item; add a reconcile step when code and text disagree.
audit_note: Chen et al. o1-preview 88.2/81.9/93.3 and means 72.8 vs 79.5, Meincke Flash 2.5 -3.3, and Liu 57.7 vs 94.0 verified; the last is o1-preview vs GPT-4o (model and mode mixed), as the claim itself notes.

claim: Which written steps carry the answer can be measured by resampling: in R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on 20 MATH problems, planning and uncertainty-management sentences have the largest counterfactual effect on the final answer (100 resamples per sentence, 144 sentences per trace); forced-answer tests wrongly rank computation sentences highest.
agent_test: Offline: resample step k of S2/S4 traces 20-100 times and report the share of steps that change the answer; expect plans and revisions to matter, restated facts not.

claim: Written reasoning is only a partial record of what drives the answer: hint use is verbalised in 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (R1) of cases, less on harder questions (-44% and -32% relative), and unfaithful chains are longer than faithful ones.
agent_test: Do not use chain text alone to certify that a step was epistemic; add an intervention test.
audit_note: Minor: 25% and 39% are average faithfulness across hint types on MMLU and GPQA (lower 20%/29% on misaligned hints); Lanham supports the partial-record point qualitatively.

claim: Many code-tool calls are confirmatory, not discovering: in the dominant setting (Qwen3-235B-Instruct on MATH500) the answer was written before the call in 81% of trajectories, at 1.77x cost, and incorrect trajectories cost more than correct ones at every difficulty level.
agent_test: Log answer-before-call rate for S4 runs; a high rate suggests the call is confirmation and could be deferred to a single final check.

claim: Tool and thinking budgets can be routed cheaply without training: two no-think drafts that agree are accepted without thinking, saving 32-73% of thinking tokens with accuracy equal or higher than always-thinking in most settings (Qwen3 8B-32B, DeepSeek-V3.2).
agent_test: Pre-check for S2: sample two quick answers; skip notes when they agree; test on soft and perceptual items where notes hurt (gap 5).

claim: The first step of any gate, naming the missing unknown, is itself weak: on QuestBench models score over 80% on grade-school math but only 40-50% on logic and planning at choosing the one question that resolves the gap, even when they can solve the full problem.
agent_test: Check gate quality by having the agent write the unknown and comparing with a known-missing-fact set.

claim: The theory has been mapped onto LLM agents as a design position (acquire, transform, probe, with a value-of-information rule and a proposed benchmark) but without data.
agent_test: Label each S2/S4 step acquire / transform / probe in the trace log; the proposed benchmark could be built in small form.

claim: Having an agent write a structured account of the data before answering raises accuracy on hard spreadsheet tasks (GPT 15/20 to 16/20 own-artifact to 17/20 oracle; Claude 6/9 to 7/9 to 9/9), and a self-built artifact sometimes matches or beats a given one. Tiny N, no intervals.
agent_test: A/B: pre-answer exploration note on vs off for data-heavy items; include a 'given artifact' arm to look for a generation effect.

claim: The claim that mental images cannot be reinterpreted but drawings can (0% vs 100%, via Chambers and Reisberg/Reisberg) is too strong: with a mental-rotation step 24 of 44 reinterpreted a held image, and reconstruals occur commonly while reference-frame reversals need a hint (abstract-level evidence only). External traces help, but are not the only route.
agent_test: Do not state the 100% vs 0% contrast in schema text; instead ask for a re-frame step when rereading.

claim: Information gathering quality improves with reasoning and with a harness-built summary of what has been learned: thinking models win 93% vs 10% of partially observable guessing games at about half the turns, while in bandits only one of 48/72 prompt-model settings explored well and it needed a code-built sufficient-statistics summary.
agent_test: Give probes a code-built summary of what they returned; score probes by information gain.
